I'm getting the Windows 10 upgrade prompt constantly today, so I disabled it like this:

Right click the task bar near the time on the right hand side (don't right click the time or an icon, just the task bar next to the time)

Select to Properties

Click customize Notification Icons (at the bottom of the window)

Uncheck "Always show all icons and notifications in the task bar" (it's at the bottom of the window)

Use the drop down next to GWX to select Hide icon and notifications

Click OK twice to back out.

Admittedly, that's a bit of a puzzle to me as well. There are a few reasons they could be doing it, however.

First and foremost would be an attempt to thwart counterfeit hardware. This is probably actually a good idea, since most counterfeits are probably flawed. I suspect this problem would be much more prevalent elsewhere in the world, and Microsoft wants a billion Windows 10 devices, so they're clearly going for worldwide adoption as far as they can get, here (although that was always something they considered favorable, I'm sure). I also suspect there may be money to be made by offering a policing service to hardware manufacturers.

Another might be circumventing their control over the computer. For instance, hardware that might circumvent DRM on HDMI signals, or if there is a piece of hardware that might be used to circumvent UEFI restrictions somehow.

Another would be that this is to scare hardware manufacturers into complying with whatever mandates they may have for hardware. I remember there was at least one piece of hardware that sometime in 2014 or so had the drivers doing some pretty nasty things. I think it was a ROM programmer? I don't know for sure; I forgot the specifics. But as I recall it was put out there by Windows Update and it bricked the device if the driver suspected that it was counterfeit. Microsoft did not take kindly to that, which makes one wonder how wise of an idea it would be to enable this feature on their own OS. However, they may just want to be the gatekeeper of this functionality, and they also have a PR department that can kick into gear if they start using this.

There is also the possibility that they may identify a piece of hardware that had its firmware infiltrated with malware and they intercept it somehow in hopes of containing the damage.

Finally, they could just be keeping their options open.

In any case, I'm sure there are more ideas here. However, there are several bad possibilities and some good possibilities. That said, I'll not be a bit surprised if we don't see this come into play for quite some time. They probably want Windows 10 acceptance and dominance to be more secure and deeper before they start pulling moves like that.
